records.name: Hessen
records.current_summary: A Hessen Landtag small inquiry with the Interior Minister's answer (April 2025) records police-registered queer-hostile offences rising from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024 — a year-on-year jump of 52 that the minister's reply calls alarming.  The trend must be read with the federal BKA's own caveat: its situation report on LSBTIQ* security introduced a new reporting category that makes state-by-state comparison possible but warns that classification changes can inflate registered counts, so rises may partly reflect better recording rather than a sharper danger. The same answer notes the 2010-established network of LSBTIQ* liaison officers in every police headquarters, governed by a standing framework concept — an institutional response in place while the statistics remain ambiguous.

sources.claim: Hessen Landtag small inquiry and Interior Minister answer (April 2025): police-registered queer-hostile offences in Hessen rose from 33 (2022) to 83 (2023) and to 135 (2024, +52 year-on-year — described as alarming); notes LSBTIQ* liaison officers established in all police headquarters since 2010 and a framework concept governing them.

Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) situation report on the security of LSBTIQ* people in Germany, published with the Interior Ministry: a multi-year rise in police-registered queer-hostile offences and the new federal reporting category that makes Land-by-Land comparison possible; classification changes can inflate Land counts, so cross-Land numbers need caution.

hessenschau reports (21 August 2025) that the Hessian interior ministry's answer to a Landtag inquiry by three Grüne MPs recorded 135 queer-hostile offences in Hessen in 2024, 52 more than the previous year, among them 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult, with many victims not reporting so that a high dark figure is assumed. Interior Minister Roman Poseck (CDU) called the development 'alarmierend', attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces, and the ministry counted suspects identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings and six convictions. This is the media confirmation of the record's police-registered 33 (2022) to 83 (2023) to 135 (2024) series.

hessenschau reports (17 May 2026) from a further Poseck answer to a Grüne Landtag inquiry that Hessen police counted 141 queer-hostile offences in 2025, against 83 in 2023 and 33 in 2022 - a more than fourfold rise within four years that Poseck called 'alarmierend' and only 'the tip of the iceberg' given the high dark figure; he cited a January 2026 Kassel tram incident in which a male couple was homophobically insulted, threatened and spat on. The article notes Hessen police keep dedicated contact officers for this hate crime and the state government promises consistent prosecution. It updates the record's statistics with the 2025 figure of 141 and confirms the state's own alarm at the trend.

Resident Advisor reports (20 June 2025) that trans woman artist BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act after a male security officer refused her a search by a female officer during screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024 and told her she was 'not a woman'; Frankfurt Airport later apologised by email, said the security service provider had been instructed to investigate, and promised security staff would be trained on dealing with transgender and gender non-conforming travellers. This is a dated, jurisdiction-specific case of transphobic treatment at Hessen's main international airport - the first screening-gate incident evidence for this record.

records.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
records.current_summary: Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three Länder — with Sachsen and Thüringen — that brought a Bundesrat initiative (reported June 2026) to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act on legal gender change, proposing an 'abuse review' mechanism with objective, documentable grounds for registry-office intervention. The trigger cited is the 'Fall Liebich' — a convicted far-right extremist whose legal gender was changed after sentencing.  The initiative is an attempt, not a change: it is backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, and runs against a scheduled federal evaluation of the SBGG that the family ministry is conducting and whose SPD-led ministries consider the existing law sufficient. No standing administrative ban or documented street-attack pattern specific to this state was identified in the research pass.

sources.claim: dpa report (updated 2 June 2026): Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thüringen bring a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, proposing an "abuse review" mechanism with objective, documentable grounds for registry-office intervention, triggered by the Fall Liebich; backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, while the federal family ministry runs a scheduled SBGG evaluation.

BBC News reports (20 August 2025) that Marla-Svenja Liebich, then Sven Liebich, was sentenced in July 2023 by the Halle District Court in Saxony-Anhalt to one year and six months' imprisonment without parole for incitement to hatred, defamation and insult, and changed her legal gender from male to female by declaration at a registry office under Germany's Self-Determination Act at the end of 2024. The article records the ensuing controversy - the chief public prosecutor in Halle told MDR Saxony-Anhalt that Liebich would begin the term at Chemnitz women's prison, while German outlets including Der Spiegel questioned the change's seriousness - and notes Liebich also lost a case against journalist Julian Reichelt at Berlin Regional Court. This grounds in Saxony-Anhalt the 'Fall Liebich' that the record identifies as the trigger for its Bundesrat initiative.

DW reports (16 July 2026) that Marla-Svenja Liebich, legally registered as a woman since 2025, was transferred to a men's prison (Zeithain, Meissen district) after being extradited from the Czech Republic, with prison management saying the decision prioritised the safety of women at the Chemnitz facility. It recalls that Liebich was sentenced to 18 months in July 2023, organised far-right demonstrations since 2014 including many on Halle's central market square, was arrested in the Czech Republic in April 2026, and that a court has yet to decide whether the changes can be reversed. This documents the outcome of the Saxony-Anhalt-linked case behind the record's initiative, including the still-open question of reversing SBGG-based changes.

records.name: Wales
records.current_summary: Wales's devolved administration has publicly maintained its LGBTQ+ Action Plan through the UK's post-judgment years: the plan's standing update page was issued answering the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025, with a dedicated young-people's edition posted January 2026.  Its 'Rights, Respect, Equality' statutory school guidance (consultation May 2025) obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on the grounds of sex, gender reassignment and sexual orientation, with incident recording and monitoring and a parental escalation route. The practical facility rules set state-wide are unchanged here, but the visible institutional commitment — maintained action plan, statutory recording duties — is an official posture of inclusion at a national moment of rollback.

sources.claim: Welsh Government LGBTQ+ Action Plan document for young people (posted January 2026): part of the standing devolved inclusion programme whose update page answers the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025.

Welsh Government statutory school guidance "Rights, Respect, Equality" (consultation May 2025): obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on sex, gender-reassignment and sexual-orientation grounds, with incident recording/monitoring and a parental escalation route.

Article on the Welsh Government's February 2023 LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales, aiming to make Wales 'the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe'; it was announced in the Senedd on 21 June 2022 by Deputy Minister Hannah Blythyn under the 2021 Welsh Labour–Plaid Cymru agreement, built on 61 recommendations from the Independent LGBTQ+ Expert Panel (March 2021) and a 12-week public consultation with 1,328 responses, and funds a Grassroots Pride Fund. The government pursued a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 (gov.wales 'Banning conversion practices in Wales', May 2024). It records the surrounding UK rollback — the UK Government blocking the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023 — while Welsh NHS commissioners stated in March 2024 they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, with parents of transgender children calling for more help (BBC, March 2024). For this record: the official Welsh inclusion framework the summary describes, with dates and numbers.

Overview article stating that LGBTQ rights in Wales track the UK framework: same-sex sexual activity legal since 1967 with the age of consent equalised in 2001 and remaining restrictions removed in 2003; the right to change legal gender since 2004 (Gender Recognition Act); civil partnerships since 2005 and same-sex marriage since 2014; full adoption rights since 2005; and discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity. Wales-specific practical content: trans adults were historically referred to London clinics for transgender healthcare until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019 (BBC). For this record: confirms the legal framework and the local gender-identity clinic a trans visitor in Wales stands under.

records.name: Victoria
records.current_summary: Victoria's Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025, created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation, plus personal association; the civil grounds commenced 15 April 2026. The state human-rights commission's explainer records public incitement against a trans person becoming criminally chargeable alongside civil recourse.  A coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women in Melbourne during the pandemic — lead case Bridget Flack, missing December 2020 — found Victoria Police failed the search, and Coroner Ingrid Giles made nine recommendations including urgent investment in trans health care and reform of missing-persons risk practice; the government is reviewing them. The inquest documents a serious institutional failure; the 2025 legislation and the review process are the corrective response.

sources.claim: Official factsheet (2025): Victoria's new anti-hate laws — the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025 passed in April 2025, inserting civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958 while repealing the RRTA; aimed at equal participation and public safety.

ABC News, 29 Aug 2024: a Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people; the state government says it is reviewing the recommendations and local advocacy groups will press for implementation. Documents acute local risk factors (mental-health access) rather than visitor-facing law.

records.name: Kelantan
records.current_summary: In August 2026 the Kelantan assembly passed a new Syariah Criminal Offences Bill — including a clause making gender change an offence for persons under the state's syariah jurisdiction — replacing provisions of the state's 2019 syariah criminal code that Malaysia's Federal Court had struck down as outside state power. The Bill also carries "protection of modesty" decency offences, backed by whipping (3–6 strokes), fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years.  The sequence — invalidation by the federal courts, prompt deliberate re-enactment by the state assembly — documents institutional determination to criminalise gender transition, not a stray provision. The gender-change offence binds Muslims, including Muslim travellers exposed to syariah proceedings; the official climate it signals reaches all trans visitors.

sources.claim: Kelantan's newly passed Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 (passed Aug 2026) contains provisions on covering aurat (modesty), gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts, replacing 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 struck down by the Federal Court. Clause 15 mandates Muslims safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law. For this record: the state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning 2026.

Follow-up report confirms Kelantan passed strict new decency rules via the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 (13 Aug 2026), legislating decency, aurat-covering, and gender-change provisions; the enactment replaces 16 provisions of the 2019 enactment struck down by the Federal Court. The article also notes a related Feb 2026 first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change. For this record: confirms the new decency/gender-change legislation is now in force and being applied by the Syariah courts.

records.name: Terengganu
records.current_summary: In May 2025 the Kuala Terengganu authority erected anti-homosexuality warning signboards at several locations, including near youth-frequented areas around a state university; when criticised, a state executive councillor publicly confirmed the installations were deliberate, framing them as a "constant reminder" to steer people away from homosexuality. A prominent transgender activist and, on 14 May 2025, thirteen civil-society organisations led by a national trans-rights group demanded removal, calling the boards discriminatory hate speech.  The state also retains hudud-style penal provisions (2002) that remain inoperative because a federal statute caps the sentences state religious courts may impose — confirmed current in a 2026 review — while discretionary syariah offences and the federal criminal prohibition of same-sex conduct do apply. What visitors meet here is open, ongoing official hostility, without any trans-status-specific criminalisation documented in the surviving sources.

sources.claim: A Terengganu state executive councillor (May 2025) openly confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices installed at strategic locations in the state are intended to instil hatred of homosexual acts, saying the state wants people to consider the acts 'dirty, wrong, and to be avoided'. For this record: official state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging — a direct indicator of the hostile official stance a transgender visitor faces in Terengganu.

Thirteen civil-society organisations including Justice for Sisters (May 2025) urged the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove anti-LGBT signboards, condemning them as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law; they criticised the Terengganu state executive councillor's defence of the signboards as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals. For this record: corroborates the official anti-LGBT campaign in Terengganu and documents civil-society pushback with named actors.

records.name: Kedah
records.current_summary: In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 transgender women were singled out from the gathering and arrested, while the event's organiser was separately investigated for "encouraging vice". A coalition of Malaysian human-rights organisations publicly protested, identifying a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of trans people rather than only trans people themselves.  The raid's design — isolating trans women as a category from a mixed party — evidences enforcement capacity and willingness aimed at transgender people specifically. The surviving sources date from 2020 and document no later Kedah-specific incident series.

sources.claim: Malay Mail (30 Oct 2020): a coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups expresses concern over the probe of a Kedah event organiser for 'encouraging vice' after a private birthday party was raided and 30 trans women singled out and arrested — highlighting a trend of punishing organisers and allies of transgender persons.

The page's dedicated Kedah section reports the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014): liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex) are criminalised under sections 23 and 24, punishable by up to RM5,000 fine, up to 3 years' imprisonment, or up to 6 strokes of whipping (or any combination); a male posing as a woman in public is criminalised under section 26 (up to RM1,000 fine or up to 1 year imprisonment), while female cross-dressing is not; women convicted of musahaqah may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to 6 months under section 52. For this record: Kedah-specific state criminal law covering same-sex conduct and trans male-to-female public presentation, the direct legal risk a trans visitor faces in this state.

records.name: Bali
records.current_summary: Bali is Indonesia's most tolerant mainstream environment: 2026 travel guidance still describes a "live and let live" ethos, with gay-friendly life concentrated in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud, and no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists recorded. That informality, however, is not protection. The national penal code brought into force in 2026 criminalises extramarital sex, including same-sex relations; LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate the island "Exercise Significant Caution", public displays of affection are discouraged for all couples, and same-sex marriage remains unrecognised.  A 2025 ethnographic study of the island's trans women (transpuan) communities pointedly challenges the "refuge" framing, documenting persistent misrecognition and systemic discrimination beneath the tolerant surface. Visitors should read Bali as relatively safer by local custom — with the new penal code, conservative local administration and documented structural discrimination setting the limits of that safety.

sources.claim: Peer-reviewed article (Anthropology of the Middle East, 2025) on the 'precarious lives' of the transpuan (trans feminine) community in Indonesia based on four ethnographic case studies in Bali: documents how transpuan people navigate circumstances marked by both resistance and misrecognition and discrimination, challenging the narrative of victimhood while showing real precarity. For this record: academic ground-truth that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with precarity, discrimination, and informal resistance.

Travel guide (Gayborhood/Traven) on Bali: ranks the destination '6.3/10' with a legal score of 2.0, warning same-sex relations are criminalised in Indonesia and that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risks; advises visitors to 'keep your love a little quieter' despite the island's tolerant reputation. For this record: practical traveller-facing warning that Bali's legal backdrop (Indonesian national law) carries criminalisation risk even where the local scene is accepting.

Travel guide (Mar 2026): Bali is broadly welcoming to LGBTQ+ travellers on a 'live and let live' basis, and same-sex relationships are not a criminal offence in Bali under Indonesian national law, though the new Criminal Code (KUHP, in effect Jan 2026) adds complexity; same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia; Seminyak (Eat Street/Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, while public displays of affection warrant discretion. For this record: current, specific traveller guidance for trans/LGBTQ visitors to Bali including the 2026 KUHP law change.

records.name: Papua
records.current_summary: No trans-specific legal measure or incident series is documented for this province in the surviving sources. The security environment, however, is not neutral: rights monitors recorded 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in the highland conflict zones of the island's western half between September 2021 and early 2025, "with almost no consequences", and a further surge of military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions from August 2025, alongside internal displacement.  For any visitor — including a transgender one — contact with security forces in the highland districts carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment, and the surveillance environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned. This is a general-population security finding, not evidence of trans-specific targeting.

sources.claim: TAPOL briefing (July 2025): police and military in West Papua committed 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands (Sept 2021-Q1 2025) with almost no consequences; victims mostly males under 24 plus 7 women and 7 minors; arrests largely for alleged armed-group links or demonstrations; deaths during torture documented in operation areas; incidents catalogued on the 'Papuans Behind Bars' database.

Human Rights Monitor Papua Quarterly Report Q3 2025 (31 Oct 2025) on West Papua: documents killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and the failure of accountability mechanisms by security forces expanding across the territory, plus a healthcare crisis under scrutiny and arrests of protesters. Contains no trans/LGBTI-specific findings. For this record: indicates a high-violence, low-accountability security climate in West Papua relevant to overall traveller safety, but provides no trans-specific substance.

Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), and the page names Papua among the provinces whose trans residents have benefited (with Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung); only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained. The same page's national-framework facts apply in Papua: the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage (up to one year in prison) takes effect on 2 January 2026, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and customary laws may apply. For this record: evidence that trans people in Papua may obtain identity documents through the national outreach programme, and the national legal framework a trans visitor stands under while in the province.

flags: '138 recorded acts of torture... in Maybrat and the Central Highlands' — cited sources cover West Papua and Papua Highlands provinces, not Papua; and general conflict violence, not a trans visitor mechanism

records.name: Aguascalientes
records.current_summary: Aguascalientes sits under Mexico's federal framework: no criminalisation of same-sex conduct or trans presence, and legal gender recognition nationally remains a state-by-state mosaic that courts have pressed legislatures to complete.  The surviving audited sources document no state-level recognition law, no hostile ordinances, and no state-specific enforcement or incident series for Aguascalientes.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (HRW blocked the fetch); the underlying Human Rights Watch news feature (31 March 2025) surveys progress and challenges for trans rights in Mexico, including the state-by-state patchwork of legal gender recognition that the country dossier uses to identify the few states that have reformed.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (HRW report PDF not cached); the underlying Human Rights Watch report (March 2024) documents the human-rights cost of the absence of legal gender recognition in Tabasco - the dossier's reference case for how non-reforming states, Aguascalientes among them, leave trans people without any lawful marker procedure.

Guardian global-development report (24 July 2024) on Mexico City making transfemicide a criminal offence - the country dossier uses this reform benchmark to contrast the capital and pioneer states with the non-reforming majority, which includes Aguascalientes.

HRW's state-by-state survey of Mexico records that Aguascalientes 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people', one of the states still lacking an administrative recognition mechanism. This directly documents the record's claim that no state-level legal gender recognition exists in Aguascalientes under the federal framework.

La Jornada Aguascalientes (23 August 2026, Karla Lisseth Avalos García) reports that Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente activists (Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz, Hened Musalem) say conversion-therapy operations still run in Aguascalientes under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one of these spaces arrived at the group last year. They state trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression, and cite the ENDISEG survey showing 7.3% of the state's population aged 15+ self-identifies as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest proportion among Mexican states. This is the first state-specific documentation for this record of ongoing anti-trans violence and family rejection in Aguascalientes beyond the absence of a recognition law.

Infobae (9 April 2026, Joshua Espinosa) reports that Mexico's Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 with a project by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, ruled that Aguascalientes' Civil Code requirements for gender change of birth certificates - judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations - are discriminatory and violate privacy, ordering the state's Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honoring self-perception, with a new birth certificate issued and no marginal notes revealing a prior gender. The ruling's immediate effect is limited to persons represented by the civil association that filed the amparo. This is a dated, state-specific legal development that changes the record's 'no state-level recognition' picture by adding a court-ordered administrative route in Aguascalientes.

flags: no enacted state-level non-discrimination protection on sexual orientation or gender identity (a February 2025 initiative was still only an initiative)
